cards.title: Understanding REST Principles
cards.content:
REpresentational State Transfer (REST) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It relies on a stateless, client-server, cacheable communications protocol, almost always using HTTP.

Key REST Constraints:

  • Client-Server: Separation of concerns between user interface and data storage.
  • Stateless: Each request from client to server must contain all the information necessary to understand and complete the request.
  • Uniform Interface: Simplifies and decouples the architecture, allowing each part to evolve independently. This is achieved using logical URIs and standard HTTP methods.

cards.title: HTTP Methods & Spring Mapping
cards.content:
Spring Boot makes mapping HTTP actions to Java methods extremely intuitive using specialized annotations. Each core standard HTTP method corresponds to an annotation:

  • @GetMapping: Retrieve a resource.
  • @PostMapping: Create a new resource.
  • @PutMapping: Update an existing resource entirely.
  • @PatchMapping: Partially update an existing resource.
  • @DeleteMapping: Remove a resource.

Example mapping:

@GetMapping("/api/books")
public List<Book> getAllBooks() {
    return bookService.findAll();
}

cards.title: Controller vs. RestController
cards.content:
In standard Spring MVC, @Controller is used to declare a class that returns web views (like HTML/JSP files). However, for building REST APIs, we want the methods to write serialized domain objects directly into the HTTP response body (usually as JSON).

Instead of annotating every single method with @ResponseBody, we use @RestController at the class level.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class ApiController {
    // No @ResponseBody needed here! Spring handles JSON serialization dynamically.
}

content.text: In Spring Boot, the annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody at the class level to create REST endpoints is [blank].

cards.title: Extracting Input Data
cards.content:
REST controllers must extract variables sent by clients. Spring Boot provides dedicated annotations for distinct parts of an HTTP request:

  • @PathVariable: Extracts values from the URI path (e.g., /api/books/{id}).
  • @RequestParam: Extracts query parameters (e.g., /api/books?author=rowling).
  • @RequestBody: Automatically maps the JSON payload body into a Java Object (DTO) using the Jackson library.

Example using RequestBody and PathVariable:

@PutMapping("/books/{id}")
public Book updateBook(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Book updatedBook) {
    return bookService.save(id, updatedBook);
}

items.text: Client sends an HTTP POST request with a JSON body payload.
Spring's DispatcherServlet intercepts and matches request URI to the controller method.
HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) parses the JSON body into a Java Object.
The controller logic processes request and delegates execution to service layer.
Controller returns standard ResponseEntity containing response model and HTTP status.

cards.title: Customizing Responses with ResponseEntity
cards.content:
When constructing REST responses, you must have full control over the HTTP Status Code, Headers, and the Body.

Spring Boot provides the ResponseEntity<T> wrapper class precisely for this requirement. Instead of returning raw objects, wrap them:

@PostMapping("/books")
public ResponseEntity<Book> createBook(@RequestBody Book book) {
    Book savedBook = bookService.save(book);
    return ResponseEntity
        .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
        .header("Custom-Header", "BookCreated")
        .body(savedBook);
}
